# <mark>APHTHOUS ULCERATION (APTHAE, CANKER SORE, RECURRENT APHTHOUS ULCERATION)</mark>

<mark>Aphthous ulceration is an acute, recurrent, and painful condition characterized by oral ulcers that occur on nonkeratinized mucosa.</mark> <mark>It is the most common cause of oral ulcerations.</mark> <mark>Up to 30% of the population report experiencing recurrent aphthous ulcers, with most cases developing by age 30.</mark> <mark>One-third of children under 18 years also report having oral ulcers.</mark>

<mark>Aphthous ulcers typically present with a gray or yellow pseudomembrane surrounded by an erythematous margin.</mark> There are three recognized clinical types, as outlined in **Table 74-4**:

### TABLE 74-4 Clinical Classification of Oral Aphthous Ulcers

<mark>| Type         | Clinical Appearance                         | Prevalence   | Clinical Course                  |</mark>
|--------------|---------------------------------------------|--------------|----------------------------------|
| Minor        | One or more < 5-mm shallow ulcers           | 90%–95%      | 7–10 days; resolve without scarring |
| Major        | One or more 1- to 3-cm deep ulcers          | 5%–10%       | ~6 weeks; may scar               |
| Herpetiform  | 1–100, 1- to 3-mm shallow ulcers            | 1%–5%        | < 7 days                         |

### Etiology and Pathogenesis
Potential triggers include:
- Heredity
- Food or medication allergies
- Decreased mucosal barrier integrity
- Hematologic or immunologic disorders
- Emotional stress
- Trauma

Pregnancy is often associated with clinical improvement, while smoking cessation and use of sodium lauryl sulfate (common in toothpastes) may exacerbate symptoms.

The pathogenesis involves a cell-mediated immune response, with histologic findings showing a mononuclear infiltrate of T lymphocytes, macrophages, and mast cells, along with increased tumor necrosis factor (TNF).

### Systemic Associations
Aphthous ulcers can be an oral manifestation of systemic conditions such as:
- Acute HIV infection
- Behçet disease
- Reactive arthritis syndrome

### Classification: Simple vs. Complex Aphthosis
- **Simple aphthosis**: One to three ulcers recurring one to three times per year.
- **Complex aphthosis**: Continuous ulceration (new lesions form before old ones heal), often associated with systemic disease or genital ulcers.

### Evaluation and Diagnosis
A diagnostic workup may be indicated to rule out underlying systemic disease. A biopsy is recommended if:
- The lesion fails to heal within 3–4 weeks
- The clinical history is concerning

Histopathology typically shows nonspecific ulcerated mucosa with a chronic mixed inflammatory infiltrate.

### Management
**Topical therapies** focus on supportive care and avoiding exacerbating factors.  
**Systemic treatments** may include:
- Prednisone
- Colchicine
- Thalidomide

---

### Behçet Disease
Behçet disease (see Chap. 167) is a rare multisystem disorder most prevalent in Japan, Turkey, and the Middle East. It is characterized by:
- Recurrent oral ulcers (nearly universal)
- Genital ulcers
- Iridocyclitis
- Variable involvement of synovitis, meningoencephalitis, and cutaneous pustular vasculitis

Diagnosis requires oral aphthae plus at least two of the other findings. Oral lesions resemble aphthous ulcers, heal within weeks, and recur at least three times per year.

## <mark>Postirradiation Sclerodermatous Panniculitis</mark>

### <mark>AT A GLANCE</mark>

#### <mark>Clinical</mark>
Women with a history of breast cancer treated by radical mastectomy and radiotherapy develop indurated erythematous plaques on the irradiated skin 1 to 6 months after radiotherapy. The clinical presentation often raises concern for cutaneous metastasis, but histopathology reveals a benign inflammatory process.

#### Histopathology
- Lobular panniculitis without vasculitis  
- Hyaline collagen bundles in the dermis and subcutaneous septa  
- Inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes and plasma cells involving fat lobules  
- Lipophagic granulomas at the periphery of fat lobules  
- Lymphoid follicles may be scattered in the septa and fat lobules

#### Differential Diagnosis
- **Morphea profunda**: Primarily a septal panniculitis with thickened sclerotic septa; fat lobules are typically spared.
- **Lupus panniculitis (lupus profundus)**: Shows lobular involvement with hyaline necrosis of fat, lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, and possible germinal center formation within lymphoid aggregates.

#### Treatment
There is no specific treatment for postirradiation sclerodermatous panniculitis. Indurated nodules tend to improve spontaneously over time.

---

## Disorders Erroneously Considered as Specific Variants of Panniculitis

### Subcutaneous Lymphomas
(See Chap. 146)

---

## Weber-Christian Disease

Weber-Christian disease was historically used to describe cases of predominantly lobular panniculitis without vasculitis, accompanied by systemic features such as fever and visceral fat involvement. Synonyms included:
- Idiopathic nodular panniculitis  
- Relapsing febrile non-suppurative nodular panniculitis  

However, many cases originally labeled as Weber-Christian disease have since been reclassified with the recognition of distinct entities such as:
- **Erythema induratum of Bazin**  
- **Pancreatic panniculitis**  
- **α₁-antitrypsin-deficiency panniculitis**

Due to this reclassification, the term *Weber-Christian disease* is now considered obsolete by most authors. It is recommended to abandon this diagnosis in favor of more specific etiologic classifications whenever possible.

# Differential Diagnosis of Atopic Dermatitis

## Most Likely
- Contact dermatitis (allergic and irritant)  
- Seborrheic dermatitis  
- Scabies  
- Psoriasis  
- Ichthyosis vulgaris  
- Keratosis pilaris  
- Dermatophytosis  

## Consider
- Asteatotic eczema  
- Lichen simplex chronicus  
- Nummular dermatitis  
- Juvenile palmar-plantar dermatosis  
- Impetigo  
- Drug eruptions  
- Perioral dermatitis  
- Pityriasis alba  
- Photosensitivity disorders (hydroa vacciniforme, polymorphous light eruption, porphyrias)  
- Molluscum dermatitis  

## Less Common/Rare Disorders Predominantly in Adolescents and Adults
- Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides or Sézary syndrome)  
- Human immunodeficiency virus–associated dermatoses  
- Lupus erythematosus  
- Dermatomyositis  
- Graft-versus-host disease  
- Pemphigus foliaceus  
- Dermatitis herpetiformis  
- Photosensitivity disorders (hydroa vacciniforme, polymorphous light eruption, porphyrias)  

## Complications

### Ocular Problems
Eye complications associated with severe atopic dermatitis can lead to significant morbidity. Eyelid dermatitis and chronic blepharitis are commonly seen and may result in visual impairment due to corneal scarring. Atopic keratoconjunctivitis is typically bilateral and can cause disabling symptoms such as itching, burning, tearing, and copious mucoid discharge.

---

<mark>Infants presenting in the first year of life with failure to thrive, diarrhea, generalized scaling erythematous rash, and recurrent cutaneous or systemic infections should be evaluated for severe combined immunodeficiency syndrome.</mark> <mark>Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, an X-linked recessive disorder, presents with cutaneous findings nearly indistinguishable from atopic dermatitis.</mark> <mark>It is associated with thrombocytopenia, variable abnormalities in humoral and cellular immunity, and recurrent severe bacterial infections.</mark>

<mark>Hyper-IgE syndrome is characterized by elevated serum IgE levels, defective T-cell function, and recurrent deep-seated bacterial infections, including cutaneous abscesses caused by *Staphylococcus aureus* or pruritic skin disease due to *S.</mark> <mark>aureus* pustulosis, or recalcitrant dermatophytosis.</mark> <mark>A papulopustular eruption on the face and scalp may appear in early life.</mark> <mark>Although *S.</mark> <mark>aureus* is a major pathogen, infections with other bacteria, viruses, and fungi may occur—especially in patients on long-term anti-staphylococcal antibiotic prophylaxis.</mark> <mark>Additional features include pneumonia with pneumatocele formation, dental anomalies with retained primary teeth, bone fractures, and osteopenia.</mark>

It is important to recognize that adults presenting with eczematous dermatitis without a history of childhood eczema, respiratory allergy, or atopic family history may have allergic contact dermatitis. A contact allergen should be suspected in any patient whose dermatitis fails to respond to appropriate therapy. Notably, contact allergy to topical glucocorticoids and topical calcineurin inhibitors has been reported in patients with chronic dermatitis. Additionally, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma must be ruled out in adults with chronic, treatment-resistant dermatitis. Skin biopsies should ideally be obtained from three separate sites, as histology may show spongiosis and inflammatory infiltrate resembling atopic dermatitis.

Eczematous dermatitis has also been reported in association with human immunodeficiency virus infection and various infestations, such as scabies. Other conditions that may mimic atopic dermatitis include psoriasis, ichthyoses, and seborrheic dermatitis.

# <mark>Pathogenesis</mark>

<mark>Psoriasis is the result of a complex cutaneous immune reaction with a major inflammatory component involving elements of the innate and adaptive immune systems and abnormal keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation.</mark> <mark>Activation of antigen-presenting cells leads to the preferential development of Th1- and Th17-type T cells that migrate into and proliferate within the skin.</mark> <mark>Homing mechanisms involve a variety of surface receptors and chemotactic factors, such as IL-8 and the cutaneous T-cell-attracting cytokine (CCL27).</mark> <mark>Several mediators have been identified that orchestrate many of the changes typical of psoriasis, including IL-12 and IL-23, TNF-α, and interferon γ (IFN-γ).</mark> <mark>In addition to epidermal hyperparakeratosis, angiogenesis leading to capillary abnormalities in the upper dermis, and a lymphocytic infiltrate, the histopathological changes seen in psoriasis include a marked influx of neutrophils, which may form sterile abscesses in the epidermis (i.e., so-called Munro's microabscesses).</mark>

# <mark>Clinical Features</mark>

## Plaque-Type Psoriasis

Plaque-type psoriasis, which is the focus of these guidelines, is the most common clinical form of the disease, accounting for more than 80% of all cases. This variant is characterized by sharply demarcated erythematous and scaly plaques, typically located on the extensor surfaces of the extremities. Lesions may remain stable for long periods or progress to involve larger areas of the body.

## <mark>Guttate Psoriasis</mark>

<mark>Guttate psoriasis presents with small, widely distributed erythematous papules with mild scaling.</mark> <mark>It is often the first clinical manifestation of psoriasis, particularly when triggered by a streptococcal infection.</mark> <mark>A later transition to plaque psoriasis may occur.</mark>

## Intertriginous Psoriasis

Intertriginous psoriasis is defined by plaques located predominantly or exclusively in major skin folds, such as the axillae, abdominal folds, submammary area, and inguinal/gluteal clefts.

## Inverse Psoriasis

Inverse psoriasis is characterized by plaques primarily affecting flexural areas without involvement of the typical predilection sites (e.g., extensor surfaces). It often overlaps with intertriginous psoriasis in clinical presentation.

## Pustular Psoriasis

Pustular psoriasis manifests in several clinical subtypes. Generalized pustular psoriasis (also known as von Zumbusch psoriasis) is characterized by the widespread appearance of initially scattered, then confluent pustules, often accompanied by fever and generalized lymphadenopathy.

## Palmoplantar Pustulosis

Palmoplantar pustulosis is a genetically distinct condition that may represent a separate disease entity. It is characterized by the presence of fresh yellow or older brownish pustules that occur exclusively on the palms and/or soles.

## Acrodermatitis Continua Suppurativa (Hallopeau)

This rare variant of pustular psoriasis is marked by pustules with severe inflammation at the tips of the fingers and/or toes, often rapidly leading to nail matrix damage and nail loss. Over time, destruction of the distal phalanges may occur.

# Diagnostic Approach

The diagnosis of psoriasis vulgaris is primarily based on the clinical appearance of skin lesions. Auspitz's sign—multiple fine bleeding points observed when psoriatic scale is removed—may be present in scaly plaques. Involvement of typical predilection sites and the presence of nail changes support the diagnosis. 

Psoriasis can sometimes be difficult to differentiate from nummular eczema, tinea, or cutaneous lupus. Guttate psoriasis may resemble pityriasis rosea, and mycosis fungoides should be excluded in atypical cases. For intertriginous lesions, differential diagnoses include intertrigo and candidiasis. In uncertain cases, histopathological examination of a skin biopsy taken from the edge of a representative lesion may be required to confirm the diagnosis.

# Severity Assessment

Several tools are available for assessing the severity of plaque psoriasis. The most widely used is the Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI).

# <mark>Treatment of papulopustular rosacea</mark>

<mark>Inflammatory lesions such as papules and pustules, as well as erythema, occur in subtype II rosacea.</mark> <mark>In mild manifestations, topical treatments alone can be effective.</mark> <mark>For more severe cases, systemic treatment or a combination of topical and systemic therapies are recommended.</mark>

## <mark>Topical treatment of papulopustular rosacea</mark>

### <mark>Metronidazole</mark>  
<mark>Metronidazole (MTZ) is a nitroimidazole antibiotic.</mark> <mark>For subtype II rosacea, 0.75–1% cream or gel is most commonly used and should be applied twice daily.</mark> <mark>In Europe, multiple metronidazole formulations are available.</mark> <mark>However, studies have shown no significant difference in efficacy between 0.75% and 1% concentrations, and it remains unclear whether the higher dose offers improved outcomes.</mark> <mark>The efficacy of MTZ has been confirmed in multiple double-blind studies.</mark> <mark>Compared to azelaic acid (AZA), MTZ shows similar or slightly inferior results in reducing facial erythema, though it is generally considered better tolerated.</mark> <mark>In a head-to-head trial with pimecrolimus 1%, both agents reduced erythema equally, but neither improved telangiectasias.</mark> <mark>The maximum reduction in lesion count is typically observed around 6 weeks.</mark> <mark>One randomized double-blind trial (n = 51) found MTZ to have similar efficacy to oral (oxy)tetracycline, with improvement seen in 90% of patients in both groups.</mark>

<mark>**Conclusion:** Metronidazole is recommended (A) for subtype II rosacea patients.</mark>

### Tacrolimus  
A single study involving 24 patients with subtype I and II rosacea showed no reduction in papule count, although some improvement in erythema was observed.

**Conclusion:** Tacrolimus is not recommended (D) for subtype II rosacea patients.

### Azelaic acid  
Azelaic acid is a saturated dicarboxylic acid that inhibits the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and suppresses pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α. It also downregulates phosphorylation of ERK1/2 and p38, and inhibits UV-induced NF-κB activation. Additionally, azelaic acid induces PPARγ, which helps modulate inflammatory responses. Multiple randomized, double-blind, multicenter studies have demonstrated its efficacy in treating subtype II rosacea, with significant improvements in both erythema and inflammatory lesions.

**Conclusion:** Azelaic acid is recommended (A) for subtype II rosacea patients.

### Ivermectin  
Ivermectin is a broad-spectrum antiparasitic agent. In a phase 3, investigator-blinded, randomized, parallel-group trial (n = 962), ivermectin 1% cream demonstrated superiority over metronidazole 0.75% cream in reducing inflammatory lesions. It is now approved and available in Switzerland, many European countries, and the USA.

**Conclusion:** We recommend the use of topical ivermectin (A) for subtype II rosacea patients.

### Pimecrolimus  
Pimecrolimus 1%, a calcineurin inhibitor, has been used in the treatment of subtype II rosacea. A placebo-controlled, randomized trial (n = 40) showed efficacy, though no superiority over metronidazole 1% cream was observed. Pimecrolimus 1% also showed some benefit in case reports of granulomatous rosacea. However, flares and increased facial erythema after alcohol consumption have been reported with calcineurin inhibitor use. There are also reports of pimecrolimus potentially inducing rosacea-like symptoms.

**Conclusion:** Pimecrolimus can be considered (A) for subtype II rosacea patients, but with caution due to potential adverse effects and risk of flare.

# <mark>Rosacea Therapy and Classification</mark>

<mark>Rosacea therapy may include barrier protection practices, topical antimicrobials, oral antibiotics, retinoids, intense pulsed light, and vascular laser modalities for adequate long-term control of symptoms.</mark>

<mark>The Plewig-Kligman classification system describes rosacea progression through stages, with stage III corresponding to phymatous changes.</mark> <mark>In contrast, the National Rosacea Society (NRS) classification states that rosacea does not necessarily progress from one sub-type to another, but that sub-types may overlap in the same individual.</mark> <mark>A provisional grading system was developed by the NRS Expert Committee to standardize clinical assessment.</mark> <mark>Rosacea severity evaluations should also consider the psychological, social, and occupational impact of the condition, as well as individual treatment responsiveness.</mark>

# Epidemiology

Although the exact prevalence of rosacea is unknown, it is considered common, particularly in Caucasian populations. While the majority of cases occur in fair-skinned individuals, rosacea can also affect people of African and Asian descent. The NRS estimates that rosacea affects approximately 14 million Americans. It occurs in both men and women, with onset typically after age 30. However, cases have been reported in children, adolescents, and young adults.

# Etiology and Pathogenesis

The clinical variability among rosacea sub-types suggests possible differences in etiology and pathophysiology. These may involve facial vascular reactivity, dermal connective tissue structure or composition, extracellular matrix changes, pilosebaceous unit abnormalities, microbial colonization, or a combination of factors that alter the skin’s response to triggers.

Rosacea is unmasked or exacerbated by chronic, repeated exposure to triggers—particularly those that induce flushing. Common triggers include:
- Temperature extremes (hot or cold)
- Sunlight
- Wind
- Hot beverages
- Exercise
- Spicy foods
- Alcohol
- Emotional stress
- Cosmetics and topical irritants
- Menopausal flushing
- <mark>Flushing</mark>-inducing medications

Flush reactions are mediated by both neural and humoral mechanisms and are typically confined to the face. This facial predominance is attributed to higher baseline facial blood flow and a more superficial, extensive cutaneous vascular network compared to other body areas.

Histologic studies show dermal matrix degeneration and endothelial damage in rosacea. Contributing factors may include increased vascular permeability, impaired clearance of inflammatory mediators, or photodamaged connective tissue altering vascular and lymphatic support in the dermis. These changes can lead to chronic inflammation and persistent erythema on facial convexities in susceptible individuals.

Sun exposure is considered a contributing factor, though not sufficient alone. Solar elastosis is often present in rosacea-affected skin. However, rosacea is not more prevalent in outdoor workers, non-facial sun-damaged skin does not develop rosacea features, and photoprovocation studies do not show increased sensitivity to acute UV exposure in rosacea patients.

The mechanism of action of oral and topical antimicrobials in rosacea—whether anti-inflammatory or antimicrobial—remains debated. The role of commensal microbes such as *Propionibacterium acnes* and *Demodex folliculorum* in triggering folliculocentric inflammation is controversial. It is unclear if these organisms directly cause inflammatory papules or if a hypersensitivity reaction to the microbes or associated bacteria (e.g., *Bacillus oleronius*) is involved.

Evidence supporting a microbe-driven mechanism in papulopustular rosacea (PPR) includes:
- Poor response of rosacea lesions to corticosteroids and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
- Superior efficacy of oral tetracyclines
- Effectiveness of benzoyl peroxide in patients who tolerate it

It remains uncertain whether clinical improvement in PPR requires a quantitative reduction in *P. acnes*.

# Clinical Features

<mark>**Erythematotelangiectatic rosacea (ETR)** is characterized by:</mark>
- <mark>Persistent facial erythema</mark>
- Flushing
- <mark>Telangiectasia</mark>
- <mark>Central facial edema</mark>
- <mark>Burning and stinging sensations</mark>
- <mark>Skin roughness or scaling</mark>

<mark>These signs and symptoms may occur in various combinations.</mark> <mark>ETR is classified into mild, moderate, and severe sub-types based on clinical presentation.</mark>

## <mark>Topical Therapy for Rosacea</mark>

<mark>Several topical agents have demonstrated efficacy in clearing inflammatory papules and pustules and reducing erythema when applied once daily.</mark> <mark>Twice-daily application or combination therapy may be required if monotherapy is insufficient.</mark>

- **Metronidazole** and **azelaic acid** are classified as pregnancy category B.  
- <mark>**Sodium sulfacetamide/sulfur** is pregnancy category C.</mark>  
- <mark>Azelaic acid may cause initial tingling or burning, which typically resolves with continued use.</mark>  
- Sodium sulfacetamide/sulfur **medicated cleansers** are better tolerated in patients with sensitive skin compared to "leave-on" formulations, which may exacerbate stinging and burning.  
- Daily use of a **barrier repair emollient** is recommended to support skin integrity.

### Off-Label Topical Treatments

Common off-label topical agents include:

- **Benzoyl peroxide**: Effective for papules and pustules but may irritate sensitive skin.  
- <mark>**Clindamycin**: Twice-daily topical clindamycin has shown superior pustule clearance compared to oral tetracycline in one study.</mark>  
- **Erythromycin**: Used topically, though evidence is limited.  
- **Calcineurin inhibitors** (tacrolimus ointment, pimecrolimus cream): Most effective for steroid-induced perioral dermatitis but may benefit select rosacea patients, particularly those with inflammatory lesions.

### Adjunctive Manual Therapy

Facial massage, performed according to **Soybe’s technique**, may serve as an adjunctive treatment:

- Begins at the central face (glabella and nose).  
- Involves sweeping motions toward the inferolateral face (mandibles and lateral neck) in the direction of lymphatic flow.  
- Aims to mobilize edema and accelerate clearance of dermal inflammation.

### Topical Retinoids

- **Tretinoin cream** promotes connective tissue remodeling and reduces dermal inflammation over time.  
- Small clinical studies support the use of topical retinoids in rosacea.  
- Clinical improvement is delayed, typically requiring **4 to 6 months** of consistent use.  
- Potential for irritation and theoretical concerns about angiogenesis have limited their use, though long-term data do not support an increased risk of telangiectasia.  
- Retinoids inhibit **vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)** production via anti-AP1 activity in keratinocytes.  
- Tolerability can be improved by:
  - Gradual introduction of the retinoid.  
  - Concomitant use of barrier repair emollients.  
- Particularly valuable for **long-term maintenance** therapy.

---

## <mark>Oral Therapy for Rosacea</mark>

Topical management is generally preferred to minimize risks of antimicrobial resistance and systemic side effects. <mark>However, oral therapies are used off-label and can provide rapid symptom control, especially in moderate to severe cases.</mark>

### General Considerations

- Oral antibiotics should be used short-term; long-term maintenance should rely on topical agents.  
- Photosensitizing agents require caution due to the photodistributed nature of rosacea.  
- All discussed oral therapies are used **off-label**.

### Tetracyclines

- <mark>Effective for reducing papules, pustules, and erythema.</mark>  
- <mark>Have been used since the 1950s at both antimicrobial and sub-antimicrobial doses.</mark>  
- <mark>Faster onset of action compared to isotretinoin.</mark>  
- Relapse rates:
  - ~25% within 1 month of discontinuation.  
  - >50% by 6 months off therapy.  
- **Topical maintenance** is recommended after oral treatment.  
- **Contraindicated** in pregnant women and those planning pregnancy.

### Isotretinoin

- <mark>Low-dose isotretinoin (10–40 mg daily, or <0.5 mg/kg/day) is effective and better tolerated in rosacea patients.</mark>  
- One small study showed:
  - Significant reduction in facial blood flow (measured by laser-Doppler) with 30 mg daily for 10 weeks.  
  - No significant change with tetracycline 250 mg twice daily over the same period.  
- Useful for short-term control of moderate to severe flushing or erythema.

# Environment

<mark>Environmental trigger factors include exposure to extremes of temperature (hot and cold air), temperature changes, caffeine, alcohol, hot and spicy foods, sunlight, exercise, acute psychological stresses, menstruation, demodex mites, and certain medications.</mark> <mark>There is controversy regarding whether *H.</mark> <mark>pylori* should be considered a trigger factor for rosacea.</mark>

# Cytokines

Due to an impaired permeability barrier in the stratum corneum, the release of various cytokines such as tumour necrosis factor α (TNF-α), IL-1, and IL-6 is triggered, leading to cutaneous inflammation—possibly as an attempt by the epidermis to initiate self-repair. These pathomechanisms can lead to neurological symptoms such as stinging and burning sensations.

# Antimicrobial Peptides

Recently, overproduction of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) has been identified as a cause of rosacea lesions. AMPs include defensins and cathelicidins, such as LL-37.

# Toll-like Receptors

Keratinocytes express Toll-like receptors to sense pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs). Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) and Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) have been shown to be overexpressed in rosacea skin.

# Adaptive Immune Cells

T cells (especially Th1/Th17-polarized immune cells), macrophages, mast cells, and neutrophils are present in all subtypes I–III of rosacea. Neutrophils are assumed to play an essential role in the pathogenesis of rosacea. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) and other proteases produced by neutrophils damage blood vessels, causing inflammation and angiogenesis, which can lead to telangiectasias. Recently, involvement of B cells in the pathomechanism of rosacea has also been demonstrated.

# Mites

Demodex mites, although normally present in adult skin, are found in increased numbers in many rosacea patients. A reduction in Demodex mite density correlates with improvement in rosacea symptoms.

# Blood Vessels

Vascular dilation results in erythema, which may appear transiently as facial flushing. In rosacea, the papillary dermal vasculature is dilated and skin perfusion is increased.

# Nerves

Sensory nerve endings release vasoactive neuropeptides via transient receptor potential (TRP) channels. Two calcium channel blockers and members of the TRP family—transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) and transient receptor potential ankyrin 1 (TRPA1)—are of particular interest in rosacea, as they mediate inflammatory responses. These channels are activated by spices, alcohol consumption, and temperature changes. Upon activation, TRPV1 and TRPA1 induce the release of neuropeptides such as pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP), substance P (SP), and calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), which collectively cause flushing and erythema through vasodilation. PACAP, SP, and CGRP also promote inflammation by activating mast cells, macrophages, neutrophils, and T cells.

Due to the multifactorial pathogenesis of rosacea, which is difficult to target therapeutically, current treatment strategies focus on symptomatic suppression of inflammation and reduction of disfiguring features. Clinically, four subtypes of rosacea are differentiated based on observable features and severity.

# <mark>Clinical Manifestations and Subtypes of Rosacea</mark>

<mark>Patients with subtype I (erythematotelangiectatic rosacea, ETR) present with centrofacial erythematous macules due to dilated facial capillaries, particularly on the nose and cheeks.</mark> <mark>They may experience episodes of transient erythema (flushing) or non-transient (persistent) erythema.</mark> <mark>ETR flares result from acute vasodilation and innate inflammation.</mark> <mark>With chronic vascular dilation, persistent facial erythema develops.</mark> <mark>Additionally, chronic edema may occur due to extravascular fluid leakage and perivascular inflammation.</mark>

# <mark>Malassezia (Pityrosporum) Folliculitis</mark>

<mark>Lesions typically appear on the back, chest, and sometimes the extremities in adolescents.</mark> <mark>Pruritus is more common than with typical tinea versicolor.</mark> <mark>The primary lesion is a perifollicular, erythematous, 2- to 3-mm papule or pustule.</mark>

<mark>Only appropriate culture and KOH examination can distinguish this infection from bacterial folliculitis.</mark> <mark>Frequently, biopsy with special stains for fungus is necessary, but *Malassezia* can often be recognized in follicles even in hematoxylin and eosin-stained sections.</mark>

<mark>Predisposing factors include:</mark>
- <mark>Diabetes mellitus</mark>
- <mark>Glucocorticoid use</mark>
- <mark>Antibiotic therapy</mark>
- <mark>Immunosuppressive medications</mark>

<mark>There have also been cases of recalcitrant acne vulgaris coexisting with *Pityrosporum* folliculitis.</mark>

## Box 189-5: Differential Diagnosis of Pityrosporum Folliculitis

**Most Likely**
- Bacterial folliculitis
- Acne vulgaris

**Consider**
- Candidal folliculitis
- Eosinophilic folliculitis

**Always Rule Out**
- Disseminated candidiasis
- Pustular drug eruption

# Inverse Tinea Versicolor

Lesions are predominantly found in flexural areas. They present as sharply demarcated, confluent, erythematous patches that may be confused with:
- Inverse psoriasis
- Seborrheic dermatitis
- Erythrasma
- Candidiasis
- Dermatophytic infections

# Clinical Features of Cutaneous Variants

- Equal sex distribution
- Tend to flare during summer months (due to increased heat and humidity)
- More common in tropical climates
- Favors late adolescence and early adulthood (when sebaceous glands are most active)

# Laboratory Findings

To identify *Malassezia* yeast forms:
- Skin scales should be scraped onto a glass slide and treated with 10% KOH
- Alternatively, use cellophane tape to collect scales; mount on a slide with methylene blue for selective staining

Microscopic appearance is classically described as "spaghetti and meatballs."

# Pathology

**Tinea Versicolor**
- Organisms inhabit the stratum corneum
- Usually no dermal infiltrate
- Yeast may be visible on hematoxylin and eosin staining; PAS staining is confirmatory
- Microscopy shows clusters of oval budding yeast cells (3.5 × 4.5 μm) with short, septate, occasionally branching hyphae

**Pityrosporum Folliculitis**
- Organisms present in widened follicular ostia mixed with keratinous material
- Follicular wall rupture may lead to a mixed inflammatory and foreign-body giant cell response

## Box 189-4: Differential Diagnosis of Papulosquamous Tinea Versicolor

**Most Likely**
- Pityriasis alba
- Pityriasis rosea
- Seborrheic dermatitis
- Dermatophyte infections

**Consider**
- Vitiligo
- Psoriasis
- Pityriasis rubra pilaris
- Confluent and reticulated papillomatosis of Gougerot and Carteaud

**Always Rule Out**
- Secondary syphilis

## <mark>Diagnostic Methods for Malassezia Folliculitis</mark>

<mark>Calcofluor white/Blancophor staining, which requires fluorescence microscopy, has been used for the detection of *Malassezia*.</mark> <mark>The diagnostic performance of Gram staining was evaluated in 26 patients with *Malassezia* folliculitis (MF), diagnosed based on at least two of the following criteria: (a) typical clinical presentation, (b) histopathological identification of *Malassezia* within inflamed hair follicles, or (c) clinical response to antifungal therapy.[20] Gram staining correctly identified 22 out of 26 patients, yielding a sensitivity of $84.6\%$.</mark> <mark>In the same study, all six patients without MF were correctly classified as negative, resulting in a specificity of $100\%$.[20]</mark>  

<mark>The diagnostic accuracy of potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation and May-Grünwald-Giemsa (MGG) staining was assessed in 49 patients with MF confirmed by cytological examination, fungal culture, and molecular analysis.[7] KOH correctly identified 40 patients (sensitivity $81.6\%$), while MGG detected all 49 cases (sensitivity $100\%$).</mark> <mark>Since all participants in this study had MF, specificity for KOH and MGG could not be determined.[7]</mark>

## Histopathological Examination

For histopathological evaluation, a punch biopsy is typically obtained from the central area of a follicular lesion and stained with haematoxylin-eosin (H&E) or periodic acid–Schiff (PAS). Characteristic findings include dilated and plugged hair follicles associated with a mixed inflammatory infiltrate composed of eosinophils, lymphocytes, neutrophils, and plasma cells.[6,21]

## Molecular-Based Detection

Molecular techniques such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) can identify specific *Malassezia* species and genotypes, thereby supporting the diagnosis of MF.[6,19,22–24] However, because *Malassezia* is part of the normal cutaneous microbiota, molecular detection alone cannot confirm pathogenic involvement.[6,22] PCR methods used include real-time PCR, end-point PCR, restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP)-PCR, terminal RFLP (tRFLP), and PCR sequencing.[6,22] Despite their utility, neither PCR nor MALDI-TOF MS is routinely available in most clinical settings.

## Fungal Culture

Fungal cultures can be performed using specialized media such as Dixon’s agar, Leeming-Notman agar, or Ushijima’s medium.[19,25] Culture results may support the diagnosis of MF and provide antimycotic susceptibility data. However, contamination with non-pathogenic *Malassezia* from adjacent normal skin is a potential pitfall.[6,26] Additionally, growth rates vary among *Malassezia* species, which may skew results, and these culture methods are not widely accessible in routine clinical practice.[6,12]

## Wood’s Light Examination

During Wood’s light examination, ultraviolet light (320–400 nm) is applied to the skin, causing MF lesions to fluoresce with a green-yellow hue. In a study of 49 patients with MF confirmed by cytology, culture, and molecular methods, the sensitivity of Wood’s light was $65.3\%$. While this method can support clinical diagnosis, it lacks genus and species specificity (see Table 1).

## Comments on the Diagnosis of Malassezia Folliculitis

Direct microscopic examination (e.g., KOH, MGG) is a non-invasive method with high diagnostic accuracy and is recommended when clinical suspicion of MF exists. However, it is not currently required before initiating topical antifungal therapy. Although this may lead to diagnostic uncertainty, microscopic evaluation is not universally available, and delays in treatment initiation may occur. Topical antifungals have demonstrated cure rates up to $100\%$ in some studies, with minimal adverse effects (Table S5).[28,29] Therefore, in typical cases, the benefits of clinical diagnosis without mandatory microscopy outweigh the risks. Nevertheless, microscopic examination remains a valuable supplementary tool, particularly in refractory or atypical cases.

## Treatments for Malassezia Folliculitis

Evidence for MF treatment is limited to one randomized controlled trial evaluating oral itraconazole, along with several non-randomized comparative and non-comparative interventional studies, observational reports, and case series. Treatment recommendations are summarized in Table 2, with supporting evidence detailed in Tables S5 and S6.

# <mark>CLINICAL FINDINGS</mark>

A consensus development conference was held by the National Institutes of Health in 1987 to establish diagnostic criteria for neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF-1), with the goal of improving clinical research and patient care. <mark>The conference identified seven diagnostic features (Table 142-1), and it was recommended that two or more of these criteria be present to establish a diagnosis of NF-1.</mark> These criteria have proven highly effective and remain in use without modification more than 20 years later.

## Café-au-Lait Spots

<mark>Café-au-lait spots are flat, pigmented macules and are often the first clinical manifestation of NF-1 (Fig.</mark> 142-1). They are frequently present at birth and tend to increase in number during infancy and early childhood, with new spots commonly appearing throughout the first decade of life. As the child grows, existing spots also enlarge proportionally. Although they can occur anywhere on the body, they are rarely found on the face. The size, shape, and borders of café-au-lait spots are not diagnostically predictive; however, most spots in NF-1 are oval with smooth, well-defined margins.

The commonly cited notion that smooth-edged café-au-lait spots suggest NF-1 while irregular borders are more typical of McCune-Albright syndrome can be misleading and should be interpreted cautiously (Box 142-1). When café-au-lait spots overlap, the area of overlap may appear darker than either individual spot. When located within mongolian spots, they are often surrounded by a lighter pigmented halo.

The number or distribution of café-au-lait spots does not correlate with disease severity in NF-1. Additionally, the location of these macules does not predict where neurofibromas will develop.

Histologically, café-au-lait spots consist of clusters of heavily pigmented melanocytes of neural crest origin in the epidermis. These cells may contain increased numbers of "giant" melanosomes or melanin macroglobules, but these findings are not specific to NF-1 and have no diagnostic utility in biopsy specimens.

### TABLE 142-1 Diagnostic Criteria for Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF-1)<sup>a</sup>

- Six or more café-au-lait macules >5 mm in greatest diameter in prepubertal individuals or >15 mm in postpubertal individuals  
- Two or more neurofibromas of any type, or one plexiform neurofibroma  
- Freckling in the axillary or inguinal regions  
- Optic pathway glioma  
- Two or more iris Lisch nodules  
- A distinctive osseous lesion, such as sphenoid dysplasia or thinning of the long bone cortex, with or without pseudarthrosis  
- A first-degree relative (parent, sibling, or offspring) with NF-1 by the above criteria  

<mark><sup>a</sup> Two or more criteria required for diagnosis.</mark>

### Box 142-1  
**Differential Diagnosis of Syndromes Associated with Multiple Café-au-Lait Spots<sup>a</sup>**

- Neurofibromatosis type 1  
- Familial café-au-lait spots  
- LEOPARD syndrome (multiple lentigines, electrocardiographic abnormalities, ocular hypertelorism, pulmonary stenosis, abnormalities of the genitalia, growth retardation, deafness)  
- Neurofibromatosis type 2  
- McCune-Albright syndrome (polyostotic fibrous dysplasia)  
- Tuberous sclerosis  
- Fanconi anemia  
- Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B  
- Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba syndrome  
- Bloom syndrome  
- Ataxia-telangiectasia  

<sup>a</sup> Listed in approximate order of typical number of café-au-lait macules.

# THE NEUROFIBROMATOSES

# AT A GLANCE

<mark>Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF-1), an autosomal dominant condition, occurs at an incidence of 1 in 3000 live births.</mark> <mark>Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF-2), a separate autosomal dominant disorder, occurs at an incidence of 1 in 40,000 live births.</mark>

<mark>NF-1 can be diagnosed clinically if two of the following features are present:</mark>  
- <mark>Six or more café-au-lait spots (larger than 0.5 cm in children, larger than 1.5 cm in adults)</mark>  
- <mark>Intertriginous freckling</mark>  
- <mark>Two or more cutaneous neurofibromas or one plexiform neurofibroma</mark>  
- <mark>Optic nerve glioma</mark>  
- <mark>Characteristic bony lesion</mark>  
- <mark>Iris Lisch nodules</mark>  
- <mark>A first-degree relative with NF-1</mark>  

<mark>Cutaneous neurofibromas are softer than the surrounding connective tissue and protrude just above the skin surface or lie just under the skin.</mark> <mark>Subcutaneous neurofibromas, which arise from peripheral nerves and can be located under the skin or deep in the viscera, are generally much harder.</mark>

<mark>Plexiform neurofibromas, typically present at birth or evident within the first few years of life, may cause disfigurement, blindness (due to amblyopia, glaucoma, or proptosis), loss of limb function, or organ dysfunction through compression of vital structures.</mark> <mark>These individuals appear to have an increased risk of facial dysmorphism, mental retardation, early appearance of neurofibromas, and the presence of plexiform neurofibromas.</mark> <mark>There is evidence that NF-1 is more severe when inherited from the mother rather than the father.</mark>

<mark>The hallmark of NF-2 is the presence of bilateral vestibular schwannomas.</mark> <mark>Individuals with NF-2 are also at increased risk for developing multiple meningiomas, schwannomas, gliomas, and neurofibromas throughout the neural axis.</mark>

<mark>Segmental NF-1 involves manifestations of NF-1—typically café-au-lait macules and neurofibromas—limited to one region of the body.</mark> <mark>This results from a post-zygotic mutation in the *NF1* gene, leading to somatic mosaicism.</mark>

# Molecular Biology

The *NF1* gene is located on the long arm of chromosome 17 and encodes a protein called **neurofibromin**. Homozygosity for mutant *NF1* alleles has not been reported, likely because it is a lethal condition.

*NF1* has an unusually high mutation rate, estimated at $2.4$ to $10 \times 10^{-5}$ gametes per generation—one of the highest rates among known inherited disorders. This may be due to the large size of the gene, which spans $350\ \text{kb}$ of genomic DNA and contains 59 exons encoding a protein of over 2800 amino acids. Alternatively, the gene may have structural features that make it particularly prone to mutation.

New mutations account for approximately 50% of NF-1 cases and occur most frequently on the paternally inherited allele. Unlike many other autosomal dominant disorders, the frequency of new mutations does not increase with advancing paternal age.

Most *NF1* mutations lead to reduced intracellular levels of neurofibromin, which is sufficient to cause the clinical features of the disease. Tumorigenesis—such as the development of benign dermal neurofibromas—requires inactivation of the normal *NF1* allele in somatic cells, a process known as **loss of heterozygosity**. This two-hit mechanism is characteristic of **tumor suppressor genes**, as seen in other inherited cancer predisposition syndromes like retinoblastoma and Li-Fraumeni syndrome. Tumor formation occurs when both copies of the gene are inactivated: the first by an inherited mutation, the second by a somatic mutation.

# <mark>Unidentified Bright Objects (UBOs)</mark>

<mark>UBOs may be found in the internal capsule, basal ganglia, cortex, cerebellar hemispheres, optic tract, or brainstem.</mark> <mark>They do not enhance and are not associated with compression of surrounding tissue, features that distinguish them from neoplasms.</mark> <mark>UBOs are present in approximately 60 percent of children with NF-1 but disappear with age and are uncommon in adults.</mark> <mark>They are not associated with focal neurologic signs and are of uncertain significance.</mark> <mark>Histopathologic studies have shown that the UBOs correspond to areas of myelin vacuolization with increased water content.</mark> Some studies have found that children with NF-1 who have UBOs have significantly lower IQ and language scores, show significantly impaired visual-motor integration and motor coordination, and are at much greater risk for impaired academic achievement compared with NF-1 patients without UBOs.

# Intelligence and Learning Disabilities

Contrary to gross misstatements in the older literature, the mean IQ of patients with NF-1 is only 5 to 10 points lower than that of the general population and unaffected siblings. However, learning disabilities, defined as discrepancies between ability (intellect) and performance, are quite common, with an estimated prevalence of 30 percent to 60 percent. Although earlier reports suggested there might be a specific "cognitive phenotype" in NF-1 characterized by an excess of visual-perceptual disabilities, more recent studies have demonstrated that verbal deficits (e.g., reading) are at least as common as nonverbal disabilities in individuals with NF-1. These learning disabilities are lifelong and can affect adult functioning. Many children with NF-1 also have poor attention and impulse control and may be diagnosed with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, which significantly interferes with school performance and learning. The use of stimulant medications may have a profound beneficial effect on the ability of these individuals to succeed academically and professionally.

# Treatment of Neurofibromatosis Type 1

Individuals with NF-1 are best cared for within a multidisciplinary clinic that has access to a wide range of subspecialists. The exact physician composition of the clinic is less important than the ability to obtain expeditious subspecialty consultation. All first-degree relatives should be examined for the cutaneous manifestations of NF-1 and should undergo slit-lamp examination at the first visit to ascertain the presence of Lisch nodules. Yearly visits allow the physician to identify NF-1 complications early while providing counseling and dissemination of information regarding NF-1. Individuals and families can obtain further information from the websites of the two national support groups, the Children's Tumor Foundation (http://www.ctf.org) and Neurofibromatosis, Inc. (http://www.nfinc.org).

All children with NF-1 who are 10 years of age or younger should have yearly complete ophthalmologic examinations to look for signs of an optic pathway tumor (OPT). These examinations should include assessment of visual acuity, color vision, and visual fields, as well as funduscopy and slit-lamp examination. Because almost all OPTs arise in children in this age group, the frequency of ophthalmologic examinations can be reduced in children older than 10 years of age. Yearly measurements of weight and height should be plotted on standardized growth charts, because the earliest indication of precocious puberty may be accelerated linear growth. Blood pressure measurements should be obtained at each visit to look for signs of renovascular hypertension. In addition, the spine should be examined each year for early signs of scoliosis.

# Café-au-Lait Spots

Café-au-lait spots on the face are unusual in individuals with NF-1. On occasion, they do occur, and affected individuals may seek to improve cosmesis. Attempts to remove café-au-lait spots with laser therapy have provided very mixed results. Although total disappearance of the lesion may be achieved, some studies cite a recurrence rate as high as 67 percent. Although results with use of the Q-switched ruby laser (694 nm) have been mixed, favorable reports in a limited number of cases using either the continuous-mode copper vapor laser (511 nm) or the erbium:yttrium-aluminum-garnet laser (2940 nm) have been published. Multiple treatments of a single lesion may be more effective.

# Cutaneous Neurofibromas

Discrete cutaneous neurofibromas may be removed surgically to improve cosmesis or to prevent local irritation (e.g., from brushing for lesions in the hairline or from rubbing against the shoe for those on the foot).

## <mark>Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG) and Aspirin in Kawasaki Syndrome</mark>

<mark>No definitive prospective study has demonstrated that high-dose aspirin (ASA) therapy prevents coronary artery abnormalities.</mark> <mark>In contrast, several randomized multicenter studies have shown that high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) (greater than 1 g/kg) in combination with ASA is safe and effective in reducing the prevalence of coronary artery abnormalities.</mark> IVIG reduces both the overall incidence of coronary artery abnormalities and the formation of giant aneurysms—the most serious coronary complication of Kawasaki syndrome (KS). Additionally, abnormalities in left ventricular systolic function and contractility improve more rapidly in children treated during the acute phase with high-dose IVIG plus ASA compared to those treated with ASA alone.

The efficacy of IVIG in preventing coronary artery abnormalities is dose-dependent, although the optimal dose has not been definitively established. Administration of a single dose of IVIG at 2 g/kg over 10 to 12 hours has been shown to be superior to the earlier regimen of 400 mg/kg per day for 4 days, with more rapid defervescence and reduced coronary artery abnormalities at 2-week follow-up (though no statistically significant difference is observed at 7 weeks). <mark>The current standard of care is administration of 2 g/kg IVIG plus ASA before day 10 of fever, which reduces the risk of coronary artery disease from approximately 20% to less than 5%.</mark> The precise mechanism of action of IVIG remains unknown.

Approximately 85% of children treated within 10 days of illness onset experience prompt defervescence and resolution of inflammatory signs following IVIG and ASA therapy. However, optimal management is not well defined for children who have persistent or recrudescent fever and ongoing signs of inflammation 24 to 72 hours or longer after initial treatment.

▲ FIGURE 168-5 Approach to the patient with suspected Kawasaki syndrome (KS). ASA = aspirin; dx = diagnosis; IVIG = intravenous immunoglobulin.

<mark>For patients in whom the diagnosis of KS remains likely and who remain symptomatic after one dose of IVIG, a second dose of IVIG (2 g/kg) is generally administered, as persistent fever correlates with elevated proinflammatory cytokines and an increased risk of coronary artery ectasia or aneurysm formation.</mark> In some cases, a third dose of IVIG may be considered, although complications have been reported with high cumulative doses of γ globulin.

If fever persists after two or three doses of IVIG, intravenous methylprednisolone (pulse therapy with 30 mg/kg per day for 3 days) may be considered. However, the use of systemic corticosteroids in KS remains controversial. Several Japanese studies have reported that patients treated with steroids alone or in combination with ASA have a higher incidence of coronary aneurysms, myocardial infarction, and death. In contrast, a more recent study of four IVIG-resistant KS patients suggested clinical improvement with high-dose pulse methylprednisolone (30 mg/kg once daily for 1–3 days). In 1999, Shinohara et al. reviewed prednisolone use in KS and concluded it was associated with shorter fever duration and lower aneurysm rates; however, this was a retrospective analysis involving patients who received outdated IVIG regimens not reflective of current U.S. practices.

Small case series have described the use of oral or intravenous corticosteroids in patients with IVIG-resistant disease (after at least two adequate IVIG doses), reporting symptomatic improvement without clear progression of coronary abnormalities. Due to the limited number of patients and lack of controlled data, the true impact of corticosteroids on coronary outcomes remains uncertain. Until well-designed controlled trials are available, corticosteroids should not be used routinely in the treatment of Kawasaki syndrome.

# HISTORICAL ASPECTS

Kawasaki syndrome (KS), originally called mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome, was first recognized and described in Japan in 1967 by Dr. Tomisaku Kawasaki. He reported his experience with 50 children who had been seen during the preceding 6-year period at the Tokyo Red Cross Medical Center. These children appeared to manifest a constellation of findings distinct from any previously described disease. After this description, numerous cases were reported throughout Japan. Dr. Kawasaki's first description of the disease in the English language appeared in 1974. In 1976, the syndrome was first reported in the United States by Melish, Hicks, and Larson in a group of 12 children from Honolulu seen between 1971 and 1973. Since then, KS has been recognized worldwide in children of every racial group. The Kawasaki Disease Research Committee published the fifth revised edition of its diagnostic guidelines in 2005.

# EPIDEMIOLOGY

Although Kawasaki syndrome occurs worldwide in children of all racial groups, it is most prevalent in Japan and in children of Japanese ancestry. KS is primarily an illness of young children, with approximately 80% of patients younger than 5 years of age. The male-to-female ratio is about 1.5:1. The incidence rate is highest among Japanese children between 6 and 12 months of age, with similar numbers affected in the first and second years of life. Secondary cases rarely occur in the same school, daycare center, or household, suggesting that person-to-person transmission is unlikely. In Japan, the recurrence rate of KS is reported to be 3.9%, and the proportion of sibling cases is 1.4%. In patients whose parents had KS in childhood (0.2% of over 32,000 cases), there is a higher rate of sibling cases, increased likelihood of recurrence, greater need for intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), and more coronary abnormalities one month after onset. The rate of recurrence is highest within the first 12 months after the initial episode. These findings suggest a common exposure to an infectious agent in genetically predisposed individuals.

The incidence of KS in Japan increased from 1967 to the mid-1980s.

# KAWASAKI SYNDROME

## AT A GLANCE

Most common cause of acquired heart disease in children, with highest prevalence in those of Japanese ancestry.

### Major Features of Acute Kawasaki Syndrome

- Fever
- Acute multisystem vasculitis
- Polymorphous exanthem
- Bilateral bulbar nonexudative conjunctival injection
- Inflammation of the oropharynx
- Extremity changes: erythema of the palms or soles, edema of the hands or feet, or periungual desquamation
- Acute non-suppurative cervical lymphadenopathy (≥1.5 cm in diameter)

### Diagnostic Criteria for Kawasaki Syndrome

Fever lasting 5 or more days without another explanation, plus at least four of the following five criteria:

- Bilateral painless bulbar nonexudative conjunctival injection  
- Changes in the oropharynx: injected or fissured lips, injected pharynx, or strawberry tongue  
- Extremity changes: erythema of the palms or soles, edema of the hands or feet, or periungual desquamation  
- Polymorphous exanthem  
- Acute non-suppurative cervical lymphadenopathy (≥1.5 cm in diameter)

> **Note:** A diagnosis of atypical Kawasaki syndrome may be made in patients with fever and fewer than four criteria if coronary artery aneurysms are present.

### Complications of Kawasaki Syndrome

- Coronary artery abnormalities, including aneurysms  
- Myocarditis  
- Arthralgia and arthritis  
- Urethritis  
- Aseptic meningitis  

### Treatment

<mark>Prompt treatment with **intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG)** and **aspirin** significantly reduces the risk of coronary artery abnormalities.</mark>

# <mark>PATHOLOGY</mark>

<mark>Two-dimensional echocardiography is widely used to assess ventricular function, the anatomy of the proximal coronary arteries, and the presence of pericardial effusion.</mark> <mark>According to American Heart Association guidelines, patients with uncomplicated Kawasaki syndrome (KS) should undergo echocardiographic evaluation at the time of diagnosis, at 2 weeks, and again at 6 to 8 weeks.</mark> In selected cases, magnetic resonance imaging of the proximal coronary artery segments may provide additional information. Cardiac stress testing can detect reversible ischemia in children with coronary artery aneurysms. Coronary arteriography is typically reserved for patients with persistent echocardiographic abnormalities or symptoms of myocardial ischemia. It is valuable for visualizing coronary artery stenoses and assessing the extent of collateral vessel formation.

Extensive gross and microscopic pathological studies have been conducted in autopsies of KS patients who died during various phases of the illness. <mark>The overall case fatality rate for KS is approximately 0.4%, with most deaths attributable to cardiovascular complications.</mark> The pathological course of KS is divided into four stages based on the duration of illness at the time of death.

## Stage 1 (0 to 9 days after onset)
- Characterized by acute vasculitis and perivascularitis of small blood vessels.
- Microscopic findings include endothelial activation and endothelial cell damage.
- Infiltration of neutrophils and mononuclear cells (activated T cells and monocytes/macrophages) is present.
- Expression of MHC class II antigens on coronary arterial endothelium is observed in KS but not in normal controls.
- Cytokines such as interferon-γ (a potent inducer of MHC class II), IL-1, and TNF-α play key roles in inducing leukocyte adhesion molecules.
- These findings suggest that cytokine-mediated endothelial antigen expression contributes significantly to disease pathogenesis.
- In larger arteries, inflammation initially involves the intima and vasa vasorum, with relative sparing of the media.
- Additional findings may include pericarditis, myocarditis, inflammation of the atrioventricular conduction system, and endocarditis with valvulitis.

## Stage 2 (12 to 25 days after onset)
- Marked infiltration of inflammatory cells extends into the media of coronary and other medium-sized arteries.
- Aneurysm formation begins, often accompanied by thrombosis.
- Destruction of the vessel wall is thought to result from the release of proteolytic enzymes and inflammatory mediators into the arterial media.

## Stage 3 (28 to 31 days after onset)
- Acute inflammation begins to subside.
- Granulation tissue forms in the coronary arteries.

## Stage 4 (40 days to 4 years after onset)
- Chronic phase characterized by scar formation, organization of thrombi, intimal proliferation, and neoangiogenesis.
- These processes may continue for years and can lead to severe stenosis of the coronary arteries and other medium-sized vessels.

It is important to note that while coronary arteries are consistently involved in KS, virtually any medium- or large-sized blood vessel can be affected, as demonstrated in autopsy studies. Aneurysms have been reported in the femoral, iliac, renal, axillary, and brachial arteries. KS is a systemic vasculitis primarily affecting small- and medium-sized blood vessels. However, cutaneous vasculitis is not a prominent clinical feature.

# <mark>Major Features and Complications of Kawasaki Syndrome</mark>

## <mark>Clinical Features of Acute Kawasaki Syndrome</mark>

- <mark>**Fever**</mark>  
- <mark>**Acute multisystem vasculitis**</mark>  
- <mark>**Polymorphous exanthem**</mark>  
- <mark>**Bilateral bulbar nonexudative conjunctival injection**</mark>  
- <mark>**Inflammation of the oropharynx**</mark>  
- <mark>**Erythema of the palms or soles, edema of the hands or feet, or periungual desquamation**</mark>  
- <mark>**Acute non-suppurative cervical lymphadenopathy** (≥1.5 cm in diameter)</mark>

## <mark>Complications of Kawasaki Syndrome</mark>

- <mark>**Coronary artery abnormalities**, including aneurysms</mark>  
- <mark>**Myocarditis**</mark>  
- <mark>**Arthralgia and arthritis**</mark>  
- <mark>**Urethritis**</mark>  
- <mark>**Aseptic meningitis**</mark>

<mark>Prompt treatment with **intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG)** and **aspirin (ASA)** significantly reduces the risk of coronary artery abnormalities.</mark>

## <mark>Epidemiology</mark>

<mark>Nationwide epidemics with wave-like spread occurred in Japan in **1979, 1982**, and **late 1985 to early 1986**.</mark> Since the mid-1980s, the incidence of Kawasaki syndrome (KS) in Japan has steadily increased, with the **1998 incidence more than 1.5 times higher than in 1987**. The endemic annual incidence is approximately **111 per 100,000 children under 5 years of age**.

Both endemic and epidemic cases in Japan occur most frequently in **late winter and spring**, with a smaller peak in **late fall**. KS is increasingly recognized in other Asian countries. In **Taiwan (1966–2002)**, the annual incidence was **146 per 100,000**, with a peak during **summer months**.

In the **United States and Europe**, KS occurs **sporadically** or as **community-wide outbreaks**. The highest U.S. incidence is reported in **Hawaii** (hospitalization rate: **47.7 per 100,000 children <5 years**). In the continental U.S., incidence ranges from **9 to 19 per 100,000**.

- **Peak age**: 18 to 24 months  
- **>80% of cases** occur in children **<5 years**, with most under **2 years**  
- **Infants <12 months**, especially those **<6 months**, are at higher risk for coronary artery abnormalities  
- **Prevalence by race**: Highest in **Asians**, intermediate in **Blacks**, lowest in **Whites**  
- **Clinical presentation** is similar across all racial groups  

Although **antecedent respiratory illness** and **exposure to rug cleaning** have been associated with KS, neither has been consistently confirmed as a risk factor.

# Etiology and Pathogenesis

Substantial evidence supports **immune activation** as a central mechanism in Kawasaki syndrome:

1. **Activated immune cells**: The acute phase features increased numbers of **activated helper T cells**, **monocyte/macrophages**, and **polyclonal B-cell activation**.  
2. **Proinflammatory cytokines**: Elevated serum levels of **IL-1**, **TNF-α**, **IL-6**, **adrenomedullin**, and **vascular endothelial growth factor** correlate with the development of coronary artery abnormalities.  
3. **Histopathology**: Vascular lesions in medium-sized arteries suggest **immune-mediated injury**.  
4. **Autoantibodies**: Circulating antibodies cytotoxic to **cardiac myosin** and **IL-1/TNF-α/IFN-γ-stimulated endothelial cells** are present.  
5. **Response to therapy**: **IVIG plus aspirin** reduces immune activation; **aspirin alone** does not.

Despite these findings, the **exact etiology remains unknown**. KS is hypothesized to result from an **abnormal immune response to an infectious trigger**, supported by:

- Acute, self-limited course  
- Seasonal and geographic clustering  
- Predilection for young children  

Extensive investigations (serologic, culture, molecular) have **failed to identify a consistent causative agent**. At one time, a **novel human coronavirus** was suspected, but this has not been confirmed.

## Wet Beriberi and Thiamine Deficiency

A red, burning tongue and peripheral edema have also been observed with wet beriberi.

### Laboratory Testing

Diagnosis of thiamine deficiency is made by measurement of erythrocyte thiamine transketolase activity or blood thiamine concentration. The more reliable measure is erythrocyte thiamine transketolase activity before and after thiamine pyrophosphate stimulation, expressed as the percentage of thiamine pyrophosphate effect. Normal values are up to 15 percent.

### Treatment

Thiamine is a cofactor in multiple metabolic pathways, so daily requirements are based on caloric intake, with current recommendations of 0.5 mg per 1000 kcal.

Treatment can be administered intravenously, intramuscularly, or orally. For beriberi, treatment is typically initiated with intravenous or intramuscular thiamine at 50 to 100 mg per day for 7 to 14 days, followed by oral supplementation until full recovery is achieved.

## <mark>Vitamin B₂ (Riboflavin)</mark>

### <mark>Etiology and Pathogenesis</mark>

Riboflavin was first identified in 1879 as a fluorescent yellow-green compound in milk. It functions in two coenzymes: flavin mononucleotide (FMN) and flavin-adenine dinucleotide (FAD), which play key roles in oxidation-reduction reactions during cellular respiration and oxidative phosphorylation. These coenzymes are also involved in vitamin B₆ (pyridoxine) metabolism.

Recent studies suggest riboflavin deficiency may contribute to elevated plasma homocysteine levels, impaired iron metabolism, and night blindness.

Dietary sources include dairy products, nuts, meat, eggs, whole grains, enriched breads, fatty fish, and green leafy vegetables. Most dietary riboflavin is present as FAD or FMN, which are hydrolyzed to free riboflavin by brush border enzymes in the small intestine. Free riboflavin is then absorbed via active transport in the proximal small bowel.

Deficiency can result from:

- Inadequate intake
- Malabsorption
- Phototherapy

At-risk populations include alcoholics, the elderly, and adolescents due to poor nutrition. Riboflavin deficiency is endemic in parts of India, China, and Iran where diets rely heavily on unenriched cereals.

Infants of riboflavin-deficient mothers are at risk because breast milk levels reflect maternal status. After weaning, deficiency risk increases if alternative sources like milk are not introduced. Protein-energy malnutrition (PEM) exacerbates deficiency by impairing the kidney’s ability to conserve riboflavin.

Phototherapy for neonatal jaundice causes photodegradation of riboflavin. Certain drugs also interfere with riboflavin metabolism:

- **Chlorpromazine** and tricyclic antidepressants inhibit gastrointestinal absorption.
- **Borate** displaces riboflavin from binding sites, increases urinary excretion, and inhibits riboflavin-dependent enzymes.

# <mark>European guidelines for topical photodynamic therapy part 1: treatment delivery and current indications – actinic keratoses, Bowen's disease, basal cell carcinoma</mark>

## <mark>Abstract</mark>

<mark>Topical photodynamic therapy (PDT) is a widely used non-invasive treatment for certain non-melanoma skin cancers, allowing for the treatment of large and multiple lesions with excellent cosmetic outcomes.</mark> High efficacy has been demonstrated for PDT using standardized protocols in non-hyperkeratotic actinic keratoses (AK), Bowen's disease (BD), superficial basal cell carcinomas (BCC), and certain thin nodular BCCs, with superior cosmetic results compared to conventional therapies. Recurrence rates following PDT are generally comparable to those of other non-surgical treatments, although they are higher than after surgical excision for nodular BCC. PDT is not recommended for invasive squamous cell carcinoma. The treatment is usually well tolerated, but tingling, discomfort, or pain during illumination is common. Recent studies have identified patient factors associated with increased pain, enabling earlier implementation of pain-minimization strategies. Reduced discomfort has been observed with newer protocols, including shorter photosensitizer application times and daylight PDT for actinic keratoses.

## Introduction

These guidelines aim to promote safe and effective practice across Europe for the delivery of topical photodynamic therapy (PDT) in dermatological conditions. They are based on evidence from a systematic literature review (using MEDLINE) and previous clinical guidelines. A companion paper (Part II) reviews emerging and novel indications for topical PDT.

To date, topical PDT has been approved for the treatment of selected non-melanoma skin cancers (NMSC). Currently, only three photosensitizing agents are licensed for use in Europe (see Table 1):

- **Methyl aminolaevulinate (MAL)** – marketed as Metvix®/Metvixia® (Galerma, Lausanne, Switzerland) – used with red light for non-hyperkeratotic actinic keratoses (AK), Bowen's disease (BD), superficial BCC, and nodular BCC, though approvals vary by country.
- **5-ALA patch** – Alacare® (Spirig AG, Egerkingen, Switzerland) – approved for mild AK in a single session with red light, without lesion preparation.
- **BF-200 ALA** – Ameluz® (Biofrontera AG, Leverkusen, Germany) – licensed for use with red light in PDT.

Another formulation, **Levulan** (5-ALA; DUSA Pharmaceuticals, Wilmington, MA, USA), is approved in North America and some other regions for AK, using a blue light activation protocol. Many early studies used non-standardized, hospital-prepared formulations of aminolaevulinic acid (ALA), which limits direct comparison between study outcomes.

## Photosensitizers

Topical photodynamic therapy, first described over two decades ago, involves the application of a photosensitizer prodrug—typically aminolaevulinic acid (ALA) or its methyl ester MAL. These compounds are metabolized via the heme biosynthesis pathway into protoporphyrin IX (PpIX), which, when activated by light of an appropriate wavelength, generates reactive oxygen species—particularly singlet oxygen—leading to apoptosis and necrosis of targeted cells.

Selective accumulation in lesional tissue is attributed to altered permeability of the stratum corneum and differences in porphyrin metabolism in diseased cells. Photosensitizer uptake may also occur in activated lymphocytes within the lesion.

ALA is hydrophilic, while MAL is more lipophilic, potentially allowing deeper penetration into skin lesions. However, comparative studies in AK and nodular BCC have not consistently shown superior efficacy of one agent over the other.

Recent data show that **BF-200 ALA**, a nanoemulsion formulation designed to enhance stability and skin penetration, achieved higher complete clearance rates than MAL in the treatment of thin to moderate facial and scalp AK: **78% vs. 64%**, respectively.

A self-adhesive, skin-colored 5-ALA patch applied directly to AK lesions—without crust removal—demonstrated superior efficacy compared to cryotherapy in clearing mild to moderate AK.

Techniques such as iontophoresis or chemical enhancers to improve photosensitizer penetration may increase PDT efficacy but remain experimental and are not yet part of routine clinical practice.

# <mark>Topical and Intralesional Cytotoxic Agents</mark>

## <mark>5-FLUOROURACIL</mark>

### <mark>Mechanism of Action and Formulations</mark>

<mark>Topical 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) has been used in clinical practice since the 1960s.</mark> It is a structural analogue of thymine that blocks DNA synthesis by inhibiting thymidylate synthetase. <mark>Topical 5-FU is commercially available as a 0.5 percent cream carried in a microsphere vehicle, as a 1 percent solution or 1 percent cream, as a 2 percent or 5 percent solution, and as a 5 percent cream.</mark> The solution can also be used for intralesional injection.

### Indications

<mark>5-FU 5 percent cream has been approved by the U.S.</mark> Food and Drug Administration (FDA) since 1970 for the treatment of actinic keratoses in any location; 5-FU 0.5 percent cream is FDA approved for treatment of actinic keratoses of the face and anterior scalp. 5-FU is used twice daily until an inflammatory response is seen, usually 2 to 4 weeks. The 0.5 percent cream can be used once daily. 5-FU may also be a useful adjunct before cryosurgery of actinic keratoses. Pre-treatment with a keratolytic agent, prolonged therapy, more frequent applications, or the use of occlusive dressings may increase therapeutic response.

### <mark>Treatment Considerations</mark>

Irritation during treatment sometimes requires reduction or interruption of treatment and the addition of emollients or topical corticosteroids to help quell brisk inflammation. A number of approaches to decrease irritation have been devised; whether or not efficacy is preserved is disputed. Weekly pulse dosing involves applying the medication for 1 to 2 days per week for 6 to 7 weeks. Use of the 0.5 percent 5-FU cream with microsphere vehicle may allow for a more tolerable irritation profile.

During 5-FU treatment, previously sub-clinical actinic keratoses, basal cell carcinomas, and squamous cell carcinomas may respond to treatment and become apparent. <mark>In fact, the 5 percent 5-FU cream is approved by the FDA for the treatment of superficial basal cell carcinomas.</mark> Verrucae vulgaris, verrucae plana, plantar warts, and condylomata acuminata have been treated with varying response rates with topical and intralesional 5-FU. Additionally, actinic cheilitis, mucosal leukoplakia, radiodermatitis, Bowen disease, Bowenoid papulosis, and erythroplasia of Queyrat have all been reported to respond to treatment with topical 5-FU. Further, there are reports of the successful treatment of both psoriasis and keratoacanthomas with topical and intralesional 5-FU, and of infantile digital fibromatosis treated with intralesional 5-FU. Intralesional 5-FU has also been reported to be effective in the treatment of keloids and hypertrophic scars.

The systemic absorption of topically applied 5-FU is limited, with absorption selectively greater from abnormal skin than from surrounding normal skin. Microsphere-based formulations may retain 5-FU at the target site, with less drug reaching the systemic circulation. Rarely, systemic effects of 5-FU include nausea and anorexia, stomatitis, diarrhea, myelosuppression, alopecia, and cardiac and neurologic toxicity. Side effects of the topical preparation include local irritation, erythema, pain, swelling, pruritus, dyspigmentation, allergic contact dermatitis, and photosensitivity. Unusual reactions may include onycholysis, onychodystrophy, and the appearance of telangiectasias. The use of injectable preparations may be complicated by pain, local ulceration, erosion, desquamation, and dyspigmentation.

## MECHLORETHAMINE (NITROGEN MUSTARD)

### Mechanism of Action and Formulations

Mechlorethamine [methyl-bis (2-chloroethyl) amine hydrochloride] was the first nitrogen mustard (NM) to be used in clinical medicine.
